or_d_columbia_boulder.blurb: Columbia Boulder is a single large block in the forest at Carver, in the Portland and Gorge region, and it is the first big boulder you meet when you walk in. It holds 14 boulder problems with a wide spread: a handful of easy V0 to V2 lines up its main face make it a natural warm-up, then the difficulty climbs through the mid grades to a few steep, hard problems on the lower boulders and the back side, with the toughest around V8. It is also tall for the area, so expect some highball moves on the classic easy lines and bring enough pads.
or_d_columbia_boulder.parking_note: Leave the car in the circular lot at the southeast end of the Stone Cliff Inn, then go into the forest by the left-hand entrance.
or_d_columbia_boulder.approach: From the lot, enter the forest by the left-hand entrance. The boulder is the huge block immediately to the left of it, so the walk is only a minute or two.

or_3_meth_wall.blurb: Meth Wall is a short boulder wall on the west side of the Cline Falls bouldering, on the Deschutes River a few miles west of Redmond in central Oregon. It collects 14 problems across a broad range: several V0 and V1 lines that suit a first warm-up, a solid middle band at V2 and V3, and a few V4 to V6 problems including an overhanging roof and a dyno. The stone is warm orange-brown basalt and is considered some of the better rock in the whole Cline Falls area. It is a small, quick-to-sample wall rather than a destination on its own, best combined with neighbouring blocks.

or_whale_belly_area.blurb: Whale Belly Area is a small cluster of coastal boulders at Yachats on the central Oregon coast, reached on foot along the trail that heads north from the main state park area and visible from it. There are 14 boulder problems here, from very easy ones up to a couple of hard lines near V7, though the largest group sits around V3. Standouts are the turtle-shaped lines, with traverses and moderate faces that make it friendly for mixed groups. The rock is low to the ground in a scenic, open setting right by the sea, so wind and the tide can influence how pleasant a session is.

or_cool_wall_the.blurb: The Cool Wall is one of the main sectors at Trout Creek, the central Oregon crack-climbing venue near Madras and Gateway, where the rock is basalt columns split by vertical cracks, corners and stem-boxes. This sector is all trad, with 14 routes: one 5.9, the bulk at 5.10 and a good handful at 5.11. That puts it in solid intermediate-to-strong territory and is a good fit for climbers who want sustained crack technique on a standard rack. Expect pure jamming and corners rather than face climbing, and plan on a walk up the creek from the day-use area to get to the sector.

or_cline_falls_routes.blurb: Cline Falls Routes covers the roped climbing along the Deschutes River below Cline Falls, a few miles west of Redmond in central Oregon, across the highway from the state park. It is short basalt, with 8 trad lines and 6 sport routes. Most of the difficulty sits between 5.9 and 5.11, with a pair of harder sport lines in the low 5.13 range, so there is something for solid intermediates and a couple of challenges for stronger climbers. Development began on the east side of the river and has more recently spread to the west side, and the same area is better known for its extensive bouldering nearby.

or_rabbit_ears_rogue.blurb: Rabbit Ears is a pair of volcanic plugs standing out of the forest in the Cascade foothills of southwest Oregon, reached by a long drive on gravel forest roads. The rock is andesite and the climbing is a mix of bolted sport lines and trad routes, 14 in all, split evenly between the two styles. Difficulty runs from easy fifth class at 5.7 up to 5.11, but the heaviest concentration is at 5.10, so it suits solid intermediate leaders. It is a remote, quiet, forested spot more of an outing than a quick crag visit, and a high-clearance-friendly vehicle is helpful.
